claim: Kar2-sfGFP is fully functional as a chaperone
source: This protein is fully functional as a chaperone (Lajoie et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lajoie et al., 2012

claim: The diffusion of Kar2-sfGFP slows down as the levels of unfolded and aggregated proteins increase
source: The diffusion of this Kar2-sfGFP, as recorded by FRAP, slows down as the levels of unfolded and aggregated proteins, with which it interacts, increase (Lajoie et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lajoie et al., 2012

claim: In homeostatic wild type cells, the initial half time (t1/2) of Kar2-sfGFP fluorescence recovery was 8.5 ± 2.3 s in the mother compartment
source: In homeostatic wild type cells, the initial half time (t1/2) of Kar2-sfGFP fluorescence recovery was 8.5 ± 2.3 s in the mother compartment and similarly, 7.7 ± 1.9 s in the bud (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental FRAP data shown in Figure 1A,C

claim: In homeostatic wild type cells, the initial half time (t1/2) of Kar2-sfGFP fluorescence recovery was 7.7 ± 1.9 s in the bud
source: In homeostatic wild type cells, the initial half time (t1/2) of Kar2-sfGFP fluorescence recovery was 8.5 ± 2.3 s in the mother compartment and similarly, 7.7 ± 1.9 s in the bud (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental FRAP data shown in Figure 1A,C

claim: The mobility of Kar2-sfGFP dramatically decreased upon treating cells with a lethal dose of tunicamycin (1 µg/ml) in both mother and bud
source: Consistent with the previous reports (Lajoie et al., 2012), the mobility of Kar2-sfGFP dramatically decreased upon treating cells with a lethal dose of tunicamycin (Tm, 1 µg/ml), an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation, in both mother and bud (t1/2 = 25.6 ± 9.8 s and 23.4 ± 10.1 s, respectively, after 2 hr, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Lajoie et al., 2012

claim: When cells were treated with a non-lethal dose of tunicamycin (0.5 µg/ml for 2 hr), Kar2-sfGFP diffusion slowed down with incubation time in the mother cell
source: However, when cells where treated with a non-lethal dose of the drug but for a longer time (0.5 µg/ml for 2 hr), to let misfolded proteins progressively accumulate, the situation was quite different (Figure 1B). Kar2-sfGFP diffusion slowed down with the incubation time in tunicamycin (t1/2 = 15.1 ± 6.8 after 1 hr and t1/2 = 20.7 ± 9.7 s after 2 hr, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental FRAP data shown in Figure 1B,C

claim: Kar2-sfGFP diffusion remained quick in the bud after tunicamycin treatment (0.5 µg/ml)
source: Whereas Kar2-sfGFP diffusion was clearly slowed down in the mother cell, it remained quick in the bud (t1/2 = 11.4 ± 4.8 s after 1 hr and t1/2 = 11.1 ± 4.3 s after 2 hr, Figure 1C), indicating that misfolded proteins accumulated slowly in the mother cell and did not invade the bud.
evidence: Supported by experimental FRAP data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Misfolded proteins accumulated slowly in the mother cell and did not invade the bud
source: Whereas Kar2-sfGFP diffusion was clearly slowed down in the mother cell, it remained quick in the bud (t1/2 = 11.4 ± 4.8 s after 1 hr and t1/2 = 11.1 ± 4.3 s after 2 hr, Figure 1C), indicating that misfolded proteins accumulated slowly in the mother cell and did not invade the bud.
evidence: Inferred from differential Kar2-sfGFP mobility between mother and bud compartments

claim: T1/2 in the mother part of yos9Δ mutant cells was 13.3 ± 4 s
source: T1/2 in the mother part of yos9Δ mutant cells was 13.3 ± 4 s and 18.8 ± 7.4 s in hrd3Δ mutant cells (Figure 1C), showing that Kar2-sfGFP dynamics were significantly slower than in the mother part of unstressed wild type cells (t1/2 = 8.1 ± 2.2 s).
evidence: Supported by experimental FRAP data shown in Figure 1C

claim: T1/2 in the mother part of hrd3Δ mutant cells was 18.8 ± 7.4 s
source: T1/2 in the mother part of yos9Δ mutant cells was 13.3 ± 4 s and 18.8 ± 7.4 s in hrd3Δ mutant cells (Figure 1C), showing that Kar2-sfGFP dynamics were significantly slower than in the mother part of unstressed wild type cells (t1/2 = 8.1 ± 2.2 s).
evidence: Supported by experimental FRAP data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Kar2-sfGFP dynamics were significantly slower in yos9Δ and hrd3Δ mutant cells than in unstressed wild type cells
source: T1/2 in the mother part of yos9Δ mutant cells was 13.3 ± 4 s and 18.8 ± 7.4 s in hrd3Δ mutant cells (Figure 1C), showing that Kar2-sfGFP dynamics were significantly slower than in the mother part of unstressed wild type cells (t1/2 = 8.1 ± 2.2 s).
evidence: Supported by experimental FRAP data shown in Figure 1C

claim: T1/2 of Kar2-sfGFP was comparable in the buds of yos9Δ and hrd3Δ mutant cells to those of untreated wild type cells
source: As observed with tunicamycin (Tm), t1/2 of Kar2-sfGFP was comparable in the buds of the yos9Δ (7.3 ± 2.9 s) and hrd3Δ mutant cells (8.4 ± 2.3 s) and those of untreated wild type cells (8.0 ± 2.0 s, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental FRAP data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Impairing protein quality control in the ER by deleting YOS9 or HRD3 leads to a measurable increase in misfolded proteins in the mother part of the cell over time, but little in the bud
source: Therefore, impairing protein quality control in the ER by deleting YOS9 or HRD3 leads to a measurable increase in misfolded proteins in the mother part of the cell over time, but little in the bud.
evidence: Inferred from Kar2-sfGFP mobility data in yos9Δ and hrd3Δ mutants

claim: The low abundance of misfolded proteins in the bud compared to the mother is not due to a more potent ERAD pathway in the bud
source: Since the yos9Δ and hrd3Δ mutant cells are also defective in ER associated degradation of misfolded proteins (ERAD), this data excludes the possibility that the low abundance of misfolded proteins in the bud compared to the mother is due to a more potent ERAD pathway in the bud.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ERAD-defective mutants still show asymmetric distribution of misfolded proteins

claim: CPY*-GFP accumulated up to high levels in mother cells, but not in their buds
source: Over time, CPY*-GFP accumulated up to high levels in mother cell, but not in their buds.
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations described in the text

claim: Cells that underwent budding with high levels of CPY*-GFP in the ER in the mother cell showed no or very low levels of GFP signal in their growing bud
source: Even cells that underwent budding with high levels of CPY*-GFP in the ER in the mother cell showed no or very low levels of GFP signal in their growing bud (Figure 1D, see also Figure 6C, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 6C

claim: Prolonged over-expression of CPY*-GFP led to the formation of strongly fluorescent dots in the mother cell that progressively became static
source: Prolonged over-expression of CPY*-GFP lead to the formation of strongly fluorescent dots in the mother cell that progressively became static.
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations described in the text

claim: CPY*-GFP aggregates recovered fluorescence from 37% ± 5.4% 10s after bleaching to 53% ± 10.4% 5 min after bleaching
source: The aggregates did recover some fluorescence (from 37% ± 5.4% 10s after bleaching to 53% ± 10.4% 5 min after bleaching, n = 10 cells, Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The dynamics of CPY*-GFP aggregates is rather slow
source: The aggregates did recover some fluorescence (from 37% ± 5.4% 10s after bleaching to 53% ± 10.4% 5 min after bleaching, n = 10 cells, Figure 1E). Therefore, the dynamics of the aggregates themselves is rather slow.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP recovery data shown in Figure 1E

claim: CPY*-GFP dots remained in the mother cell during budding
source: Following the cells that underwent budding, we observed that the CPY*-GFP dots remained in the mother cell (Figure 6C).

claim: Buds started to form CPY*-GFP dots themselves only after they had separated from their mother
source: The buds started to form dots themselves only after they had separated from their mother.

claim: No CPY*-GFP aggregate or otherwise misfolded material appeared to diffuse from the mother cell into its bud
source: Thus, no aggregate or otherwise misfolded material appeared to diffuse from the mother cell into its bud.
evidence: Inferred from time-lapse microscopy observations

claim: Sec61-2 misfolds and is rapidly degraded at high temperature
source: At high temperature, Sec61-2 misfolds and is rapidly degraded.

claim: Sec61-2-GFP levels were already low at permissive temperature and rapidly decreased upon incubation at 37°C
source: Its levels were already low at permissive temperature, and rapidly decreased upon incubation at 37°C as already shown for the untagged mutant protein (Bordallo et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citation to Bordallo et al., 1998

claim: Sec61-2 is significantly misfolded even at permissive temperature
source: We rationalized that even at permissive temperature, Sec61-2 is significantly misfolded.

claim: Wild type Sec61-GFP distributes equally between the cortical ER of the mother cell and its bud
source: This index had a value of 0.00 ± 0.09 (n = 52 cells) for wild type Sec61-GFP showing that Sec61-GFP distributes equally between the cortical ER of the mother cell and its bud (Figure 1G).

claim: Sec61-2-GFP asymmetry index was significantly higher (0.12 ± 0.09) than wild type Sec61-GFP

claim: In ubc7Δ mutant cells the asymmetry index of Sec61-2-GFP reached 0.27 ± 0.14

claim: No large dots or aggregates of Sec61-2-GFP were observed

claim: Misfolded Sec61-2 is asymmetrically retained in the mother compartment

claim: Retention of misfolded Sec61-2 does not require aggregation

claim: Misfolded proteins are not shared equally between mother and bud, but retained in the mother cell

claim: The luminal reporter protein GFP-HDEL is lost with nearly the same kinetics in the bud as in the mother cell

claim: The ER diffusion barrier is specific for membrane proteins

claim: Disrupting Lcb1 using the temperature sensitive allele lcb1-100 strongly affected Sec61-GFP compartmentalization

In all these cases, Sec61-GFP compartmentalization was strongly affected (BI between 3.6 and 4, Figure 2D).

claim: Bud1/Rsr1 is a GTPase involved in bud site selection
source: The earliest event in bud formation consists in the selection of the future site of bud emergence and the recruitment of the polarization machinery. This is achieved by the GTPase Bud1/Rsr1(Bender and Pringle, 1989), which is activated at the future site of bud emergence and recruits and activates Cdc24, the guanine-nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for the Rho-related GTPase Cdc42, a broadly conserved regulator of cellular polarity in eukaryotes (Chant et al., 1991; Powers et al., 1991; Bender, 1993; Park et al., 1993, 2002; Zheng et al., 1995; Shimada et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing Bud1 function

claim: Bud1 is activated at the future site of bud emergence and recruits and activates Cdc24
source: This is achieved by the GTPase Bud1/Rsr1(Bender and Pringle, 1989), which is activated at the future site of bud emergence and recruits and activates Cdc24, the guanine-nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for the Rho-related GTPase Cdc42, a broadly conserved regulator of cellular polarity in eukaryotes (Chant et al., 1991; Powers et al., 1991; Bender, 1993; Park et al., 1993, 2002; Zheng et al., 1995; Shimada et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Cdc42 is a broadly conserved regulator of cellular polarity in eukaryotes

evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Bud1 is activated by its GEF Bud5 at the plasma membrane

claim: Bud5 is deposited at the site of the previous cytokinesis through its interaction with the septin cytoskeleton

claim: Treatment with Tm strongly decreased Kar2-sfGFP mobility in sur2Δ mutant mother cells (t1/2 = 26.5 ± 8.1)
source: Similarly, Kar2-sfGFP mobility strongly decreased in the sur2Δ and bud1Δ mutant cells treated with Tm (in mother cells t1/2 = 26.5 ± 8.1 and 25 ± 10.6, respectively; Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: Treatment with Tm strongly decreased Kar2-sfGFP mobility in bud1Δ mutant mother cells (t1/2 = 25 ± 10.6)
source: Similarly, Kar2-sfGFP mobility strongly decreased in the sur2Δ and bud1Δ mutant cells treated with Tm (in mother cells t1/2 = 26.5 ± 8.1 and 25 ± 10.6, respectively; Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: The asymmetry of Kar2-sfGFP between mother and bud was lost in sur2Δ and bud1Δ mutants treated with Tm
source: However, the asymmetry of Kar2-sfGFP between mother and bud was lost, the mobility of Kar2-sfGFP being considerably slowed down in the bud as well (sur2Δ = 19.7 ± 7.4 and bud1Δ =18.7 ± 8.8, Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: Inactivation of Sur2 and Bud1 did not affect the appearance of misfolded proteins in the presence of Tm, but caused misfolded proteins to distribute more equally between mother and bud
source: Thus, inactivation of Sur2 and Bud1 did not affect the appearance of misfolded proteins and the emergence of ER stress in the presence of Tm, but caused misfolded proteins to distribute more equally between mother and bud.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP data showing similar slowing in both mother and bud in barrier mutants

claim: Deleting SUR2 in yos9Δ mutant cells led to symmetric increase in Kar2-sfGFP mobility in both mother and bud
source: Similarly, deleting SUR2 or BUD1 in the yos9Δ mutant cells lead to the mobility of Kar2-sfGFP to increase symmetrically, that is in both mother and bud (t1/2 = 11.5 ± 4.2 and 11.6 ± 3.5 respectively, in the yos9Δ sur2Δ double mutant cells; 11.8 ± 3.5 and 12.2 ± 3.5 in the yos9Δ bud1Δ double mutant cells, Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Deleting BUD1 in yos9Δ mutant cells led to symmetric increase in Kar2-sfGFP mobility in both mother and bud
source: Similarly, deleting SUR2 or BUD1 in the yos9Δ mutant cells lead to the mobility of Kar2-sfGFP to increase symmetrically, that is in both mother and bud (t1/2 = 11.5 ± 4.2 and 11.6 ± 3.5 respectively, in the yos9Δ sur2Δ double mutant cells; 11.8 ± 3.5 and 12.2 ± 3.5 in the yos9Δ bud1Δ double mutant cells, Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Inactivation of BUD1 in hrd3Δ mutant cells led to symmetric Kar2-sfGFP mobility in mother and bud
source: Inactivation of BUD1 in the hrd3Δ mutant cells had the same effect (t1/2 mother: 12.8 ± 3.1, t1/2bud: 14.2 ± 4.7, Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: In the majority of wild type buds (53%), no CPY*-GFP aggregates were detected
source: In the majority of wild type buds (53%, n = 32 cells), we did not detect any CPY*-GFP aggregates (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Only 5% of bud1Δ mutant buds were free of CPY*-GFP aggregates
source: In contrast, only 5% of bud1Δ mutant buds (n = 36 cells) were free of aggregates.
evidence: Supported by quantification data

claim: More than 85% of bud1Δ mutant buds had 1 to 5 CPY*-GFP dots
source: More than 85% of the bud1Δ mutant buds had 1 to 5 dots, whereas 90% of wild type buds had maximum 2 dots (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6B

claim: 90% of wild type buds had maximum 2 CPY*-GFP dots
source: More than 85% of the bud1Δ mutant buds had 1 to 5 dots, whereas 90% of wild type buds had maximum 2 dots (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The increasing number of aggregates in the buds of barrier-defective cells was not due to the diffusion of aggregates into the bud
source: The increasing number of aggregates in the buds of these barrier-defective cells was not due to the diffusion of aggregates into the bud, since we never observed such an event, but to the fact that the buds started to form aggregates themselves much before they separated from their mother cell, that is, much earlier than wild type buds (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy observations shown in Figure 6C

claim: Wild type cells retained both CPY*-GFP aggregates and non-aggregated but misfolded CPY*-GFP in the mother cell
source: These results indicate that wild type cells retained both CPY*-GFP aggregates and non-aggregated but misfolded CPY*-GFP in the mother cell.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both aggregates and non-aggregated CPY* are retained in mothers

claim: Retention of CPY*-GFP aggregates was not barrier-dependent
source: Whereas retention of the aggregates was not barrier-dependent, the retention of smaller, not yet aggregated entities was.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that aggregates don't diffuse even in barrier mutants

claim: Retention of smaller, not yet aggregated CPY*-GFP entities was barrier-dependent
source: Whereas retention of the aggregates was not barrier-dependent, the retention of smaller, not yet aggregated entities was.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that barrier mutants show earlier appearance of aggregates in buds

claim: Sec61-2-GFP retention in the mother cell was decreased upon deletion of BUD1 (asymmetry index of 0.07 ± 0.12)
source: This retention was decreased upon the deletion of BUD1 (asymmetry index of 0.07 ± 0.12, n = 46 ubc7Δ bud1Δ Sec61-2-GFP mutant cells, p<0.0001 t test compared to ubc7Δ Sec61-2-GFP mutant cells, Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by asymmetry index measurements shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: Misfolded Sec61-2-GFP proteins were retained in the mother cell in a Bud1-dependent manner
source: Therefore, misfolded Sec61-2-GFP proteins were also retained in the mother cell in a Bud1-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Bud1 deletion reduces Sec61-2-GFP asymmetry

claim: Aggregation and the compartmentalization of the ER by the diffusion barriers at the bud neck are required for the confinement of misfolded proteins into the mother cell
source: Together, our data indicate that aggregation and the compartmentalization of the ER by the diffusion barriers at the bud neck are required for the confinement of misfolded proteins into the mother cell.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing both aggregation and barrier function contribute to retention

claim: Treatment with very low and non-lethal levels of Tm (0.2 µg/ml) caused dramatic effects on cellular longevity, causing most cells to die after 2–4 generations
source: When pedigree analyses were carried out on plates containing very low and non-lethal levels of Tm (0.2 µg/ml), we observed dramatic effects on cellular longevity, which caused most cells to die after 2–4 generations.
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis data

claim: yos9Δ mutant cells showed a clear shortening of cellular longevity (median life span of 19 generations) compared to wild type cells (median life span of 26 generations)
source: A clear shortening of cellular longevity was observed in theses cells (median life span of 19 generations, Figure 8A) compared to wild type cells (median life span of 26 generations).
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis data shown in Figure 8A

claim: The accumulation of ER stress in cells leads to the shortening of their replicative potential
source: Therefore, the accumulation of ER stress in the cells leads to the shortening of their replicative potential and ER stress is indeed an aging factor.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that yos9Δ cells have shortened lifespan

claim: ER stress is an aging factor
source: Therefore, the accumulation of ER stress in the cells leads to the shortening of their replicative potential and ER stress is indeed an aging factor.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that yos9Δ cells have shortened lifespan

claim: yos9Δ bud1Δ double mutant cells lived similarly long (22 generations) as bud1Δ single mutant cells (23 generations)
source: Supporting this view, the yos9Δ bud1Δ double mutant cells (22 generations) lived similarly long as the bud1Δ (23 generations) and significantly longer than the yos9Δ single mutant cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis data shown in Figure 8B

claim: yos9Δ bud1Δ double mutant cells lived significantly longer than yos9Δ single mutant cells
source: Supporting this view, the yos9Δ bud1Δ double mutant cells (22 generations) lived similarly long as the bud1Δ (23 generations) and significantly longer than the yos9Δ single mutant cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis data shown in Figure 8B

claim: sur2Δ yos9Δ double mutant cells lived nearly as long (28 generations) as sur2Δ single mutant cells (30 generations)
source: Likewise, the sur2Δ yos9Δ double mutant cells (28 generations) lived nearly as long as the sur2Δ (30 generations) and longer than the yos9Δ single mutant cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis data shown in Figure 8B

claim: sur2Δ yos9Δ double mutant cells lived longer than yos9Δ single mutant cells
source: Likewise, the sur2Δ yos9Δ double mutant cells (28 generations) lived nearly as long as the sur2Δ (30 generations) and longer than the yos9Δ single mutant cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Weakening the cER diffusion barrier is sufficient to suppress the toxic effect of the YOS9 deletion on life span
source: Thus, weakening the cER diffusion barrier is sufficient to suppress the toxic effect of the YOS9 deletion on life span.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that sur2Δ and bud1Δ suppress yos9Δ lifespan defect

claim: sur2Δ mutant cells are longer lived than wild type cells
source: However, we note that sur2Δ mutant cells are longer lived than wild type cells, whereas bud1Δ mutant cells are slightly shorter lived (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis data shown in Figure 8A

claim: bud1Δ mutant cells are slightly shorter lived than wild type cells
source: However, we note that sur2Δ mutant cells are longer lived than wild type cells, whereas bud1Δ mutant cells are slightly shorter lived (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis data shown in Figure 8A

claim: The ER diffusion barrier is not required for the retention of the aging factors limiting the life span of cells growing under optimal conditions
source: Since sur2Δ mutant cells are long-lived and bud1Δ mutant cell slightly short lived, it seems that the ER diffusion barrier is not required for the retention of the aging factors limiting the life span of cells growing under optimal conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that bud1Δ cells are short-lived despite lacking the cortical ER barrier

claim: The ER diffusion barrier becomes critical for aging only upon induction of ER stress
source: The ER diffusion barrier seems to become critical for aging only upon induction of ER stress.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that barrier mutants suppress yos9Δ lifespan defect but don't extend lifespan under normal conditions

claim: Sphingolipids, Bud1 and Bud6 function in the same genetic pathway for barrier formation
source: Measuring the barrier indices of the sur2Δ bud1Δ, sur2Δ bud6Δ and bud6Δ bud1Δ double mutants indicated that all of them showed a similar defect and the BI was not lower than the lowest BI due to the individual mutations (BI = 2.6 ± 1.2 in bud1Δ, 3.9 ± 1.1 in sur2Δ, 3.8 ± 1.5 in bud6Δ, 3.3 ± 1.3 in sur2Δ bud1Δ, 3.5 ± 1.7 in sur2Δ bud6Δ, 3.5 ± 1.7 in bud6Δ bud1Δ single and double mutant cells, Figure 9). Thus, sphingolipids, Bud1 and Bud6 functioned in the same genetic pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that double mutants show no synergistic effects

claim: None of sur2Δ, bud1Δ, or bud6Δ mutations act upstream of septins
source: In all these cells, the localization and intensity of Shs1-GFP at the bud neck was comparable to wild type (Figure 10A), suggesting that none of these factors acts upstream of septins.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Shs1-GFP localization is normal in these mutants

claim: Bud5-GFP fluorescent intensity at the bud neck was clearly reduced in shs1Δ mutant cells
source: Bud5-GFP fluorescent intensity at the bud neck was clearly reduced in shs1Δ mutant cells but was not affected in bud1Δ, sur2Δ and bud6Δ single mutant cells (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 10B

claim: Bud5-GFP fluorescent intensity at the bud neck was not affected in bud1Δ, sur2Δ and bud6Δ single mutant cells
source: Bud5-GFP fluorescent intensity at the bud neck was clearly reduced in shs1Δ mutant cells but was not affected in bud1Δ, sur2Δ and bud6Δ single mutant cells (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 10B

claim: Septins control the localization of Bud5 and hence, the activation of Bud1 at the bud neck
source: Thus, while septins control the localization of Bud5 and hence, the activation of Bud1 at the bud neck, Bud6 and Sur2 act downstream of Bud1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that septins affect Bud5 localization but Bud6 and Sur2 do not

claim: Bud6 and Sur2 act downstream of Bud1
source: Thus, while septins control the localization of Bud5 and hence, the activation of Bud1 at the bud neck, Bud6 and Sur2 act downstream of Bud1.
evidence: Inferred from epistasis analysis

claim: Proper Bud6 localization to the bud neck depends on Shs1 and Bud1 function, but not on Sur2
source: Consistent with this interpretation, analysis of Bud6-GFP distribution indicated that proper Bud6 localization to the bud neck depends on Shs1, as reported (Luedeke et al., 2005), and on Bud1 function, but not on Sur2 (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 10C and citation to Luedeke et al., 2005

claim: Sur2 is downstream of Bud6
source: Double deletion of BUD1 and SUR2 did not influence the fluorescence intensity of Bud6-GFP more than the deletion of BUD1 alone, suggesting that Sur2 is downstream of Bud6 (Figure 10C).
evidence: Inferred from epistasis analysis shown in Figure 10C

claim: Septins are at the top of a signaling pathway involved in the assembly of the diffusion barrier in the ER-membrane at the bud neck
source: Taken together, these studies place septins at the top of a signaling pathway involved in the assembly of the diffusion barrier in the ER-membrane at the bud neck, and Bud6 and sphingolipids at the bottom.
evidence: Inferred from epistasis analysis

claim: Bud6 and sphingolipids are at the bottom of the signaling pathway for barrier assembly
source: Taken together, these studies place septins at the top of a signaling pathway involved in the assembly of the diffusion barrier in the ER-membrane at the bud neck, and Bud6 and sphingolipids at the bottom.
evidence: Inferred from epistasis analysis

claim: Bud1/Cdc24/Cdc42 likely target Bud6, which in turn regulates the sphingolipid-dependent formation of the diffusion barrier at the bud neck
source: Bud1/Cdc24/Cdc42 are likely to target Bud6, which in turn regulates the sphingolipid-dependent formation of the diffusion barrier at the bud neck (Figure 10D; 'Discussion').
evidence: Inferred from epistasis analysis and pathway ordering

claim: All ER membrane proteins tested (Lcb1, Sur2, Get1, Ste24, Sec61, Hmg1) were excluded from the bud neck region
source: All of these proteins were excluded from the bud neck region, whereas dsRed-HDEL was not (Figure 11A). Therefore, all ER membrane proteins tested so far are excluded from the bud neck region.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 11A

claim: dsRed-HDEL was not excluded from the bud neck region
source: All of these proteins were excluded from the bud neck region, whereas dsRed-HDEL was not (Figure 11A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 11A

claim: dsRed-HDEL localization showed that the ER is a continuous organelle between the mother and bud
source: As previously shown (Luedeke et al., 2005), dsRed-HDEL localization showed that the ER is a continuous organelle between the mother and bud.
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations and citation to Luedeke et al., 2005

claim: The ER-membrane at the bud neck differs from the rest of the ER
source: These results suggest that the ER-membrane at the bud neck differs from the rest of the ER.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that membrane proteins are excluded from the bud neck region

claim: In wild type cells, 81% of cells totally excluded Sec61-GFP from the bud neck
source: In wild type cells, 81% of cells totally excluded Sec61-GFP from the bud neck (Figure 11B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 11B

claim: shs1Δ mutant cells showed the most prominent loss of Sec61-GFP exclusion from the bud neck (∼5%)
source: The shs1Δ mutant cells showed the most prominent loss of Sec61-GFP exclusion from the bud neck (∼5%; Figure 11C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 11C

claim: bud1Δ, bud5Δ, cdc24-4 and lcb1-100 single mutant cells showed a very strong defect in Sec61-GFP exclusion (between 27–35%)
source: The bud1Δ, bud5Δ, cdc24-4 and lcb1-100 single mutant cells formed the second strongest set of mutants, showing a very strong defect in Sec61-GFP exclusion (between 27–35%, Figure 11C), closely followed by the sur2Δ and bud6Δ mutant cells (44–47% exclusion).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 11C

claim: sur2Δ and bud6Δ mutant cells showed 44–47% Sec61-GFP exclusion
source: The bud1Δ, bud5Δ, cdc24-4 and lcb1-100 single mutant cells formed the second strongest set of mutants, showing a very strong defect in Sec61-GFP exclusion (between 27–35%, Figure 11C), closely followed by the sur2Δ and bud6Δ mutant cells (44–47% exclusion).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 11C

claim: alg3Δ and gpt2Δ mutations did not affect Sec61-GFP localization much (69–70% exclusion)
source: In contrast, the lipid synthesis mutations alg3Δ and gpt2Δ did not affect Sec61-GFP localization much (69–70% exclusion, Figure 11C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 11C

claim: Formation of the exclusion zone in the ER-membrane at the bud neck is the most downstream event in the pathway of barrier formation
source: Therefore, formation of the exclusion zone in the ER-membrane at the bud neck is the most downstream event in the pathway of barrier formation, and the only event to depend on sphingolipid biosynthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all pathway components affect exclusion zone formation

claim: Formation of the exclusion zone is the only event to depend on sphingolipid biosynthesis
source: Therefore, formation of the exclusion zone in the ER-membrane at the bud neck is the most downstream event in the pathway of barrier formation, and the only event to depend on sphingolipid biosynthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that sphingolipid biosynthesis specifically affects exclusion zone formation

claim: Sphingolipids contribute to building a specialized ER membrane domain at the bud neck, in a Bud1-, Cdc42- and Bud6-dependent manner
source: We concluded that sphingolipids contribute to building a specialized ER membrane domain at the bud neck, in a Bud1-, Cdc42- and Bud6-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and localization data

claim: DiOC6 was excluded from the bud neck region of metaphase cells similarly to ER-membrane proteins
source: Strikingly, DiOC6 was excluded from the bud neck region of metaphase cells similarly to ER-membrane proteins (Figure 12A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 12A

claim: Total exclusion of DiOC6 from the bud neck was most strongly affected in shs1Δ septin mutant cells (wt = 77%, shs1Δ = 10% exclusion)
source: Similar to Sec61-GFP, total exclusion of DiOC6 from the bud neck was most strongly affected in the shs1Δ septin mutant cells (wt = 77%, shs1Δ = 10% exclusion), followed by the lcb1-100, and bud6Δ single mutant cells (38%, 40% exclusion, respectively, Figure 12B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 12B

claim: The sur2Δ, bud1Δ, bud5Δ and cdc24-4 mutations caused a slightly weaker phenotype in DiOC6 exclusion (between 46–50% exclusion)
source: The sur2Δ, bud1Δ, bud5Δ and cdc24-4 mutations caused a slightly weaker phenotype (between 46–50% exclusion), whereas the alg3Δ and gpt2Δ mutations showed the weakest or no phenotype (between 64–73% exclusion, Figure 12B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 12B

claim: The entire barrier pathway was required for the exclusion of the lipid dye DiOC6 from the ER membrane at the bud neck
source: Thus, the entire barrier pathway was required for the exclusion of the lipid dye DiOC6 from the ER membrane at the bud neck, including sphingolipids, supporting the conclusion that barrier formation involves the assembly of a specialized membrane domain of unique lipid composition in the ER membrane at the bud neck.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all barrier pathway components affect DiOC6 exclusion

claim: Barrier formation involves the assembly of a specialized membrane domain of unique lipid composition in the ER membrane at the bud neck
source: Thus, the entire barrier pathway was required for the exclusion of the lipid dye DiOC6 from the ER membrane at the bud neck, including sphingolipids, supporting the conclusion that barrier formation involves the assembly of a specialized membrane domain of unique lipid composition in the ER membrane at the bud neck.
evidence: Inferred from DiOC6 exclusion data

claim: In wild type anaphase cells, the abundance of NPCs was reduced in the nuclear envelope at its intersection with the plane of the bud neck (67% exclusion)
source: Analysis of nuclear pore distribution, using Nup49-GFP as a reporter, indicated that in wild type, anaphase cells the abundance of NPCs was indeed reduced in the nuclear envelope at its intersection with the plane of the bud neck (67% exclusion, Figure 12C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 12C

claim: Nup49-GFP exclusion depended on Bud6 and Sur2 (27% and 35% exclusion, respectively), but not on Bud1 (67% exclusion)
source: Exclusion depended on Bud6 and Sur2 (27% and 35% exclusion, respectively), but not on Bud1 (67% exclusion, Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data

claim: Reduced DiOC6 staining in the nuclear envelope at the bud neck was observed in 64% of wild type anaphase cells
source: Similarly, a fainter, but significant effect was also observed for DiOC6 staining in wild type, anaphase cells (Figure 12D). Reduced DiOC6 staining in the nuclear envelope at the bud neck (64% of wild type cells) partially depended on Bud6 and Sur2 function (38 and 50% respectively), but not on Bud1 (68%, Figure 12D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 12D

claim: Reduced DiOC6 staining in the nuclear envelope at the bud neck partially depended on Bud6 and Sur2 function (38 and 50% respectively), but not on Bud1 (68%)
source: Reduced DiOC6 staining in the nuclear envelope at the bud neck (64% of wild type cells) partially depended on Bud6 and Sur2 function (38 and 50% respectively), but not on Bud1 (68%, Figure 12D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 12D

claim: Bud6 and sphingolipids are required for the formation of a specialized membrane domain at the location of the barrier in the nuclear envelope
source: These observations are consistent with Bud6 and sphingolipids being required for the formation of a specialized membrane domain at the location of the barrier in the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Inferred from Nup49 and DiOC6 exclusion data in the nuclear envelope

claim: Bud1 is not involved in the assembly of the diffusion barrier in the outer nuclear membrane
source: They are also fully consistent with our data establishing that Bud1 is not involved in the assembly of the diffusion barrier in the outer nuclear membrane.
evidence: Supported by data showing Bud1 doesn't affect nuclear envelope barrier
